issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette:
Tane, a 54-year-old Māori combat pilot, came for help after nearly a year of living as if danger were always one step away. The event that set everything in motion had happened during a training sortie over open water: a sudden mechanical failure, the aircraft shuddering hard enough to rattle his teeth, warning lights blooming across the cockpit, and the long, terrifying descent toward a strip of sea he had no intention of meeting. He remembered the sound of the engine changing pitch, the radio crackling with clipped instructions, and the ugly certainty that if he misjudged the glide or the ditching angle by even a few seconds, he would not make it out. He survived, but the body he returned in seemed to him to be only partially the same one that had climbed into the cockpit that day.

In the weeks after the accident, Tane found himself repeatedly circling the same conclusions. He told his wife that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that something in him had gone flat and wrong since the crash. He described feeling as though he did not know himself anymore, as if the calm, competent man he had always understood himself to be had been permanently altered in that cockpit. More than once he said, with a grim sort of certainty, that he had been permanently changed for the worse. Those beliefs did not stay abstract; they made the world feel newly hazardous. If he could no longer trust his own mind or body, then he could not trust the ordinary spaces of life either, and he began to move through them as though they might fail him at any moment.

At home in Auckland, where he and his wife had once treated the house as a place to decompress between deployments, Tane became preoccupied with exits, windows, and doorways. Before settling on the couch, he would scan the room and quietly identify the fastest route out. In restaurants he chose seats with his back to a wall and eyes on the entrance, and even in familiar places he stayed on guard until he had mapped the nearest escape route. He found that he felt most uneasy in enclosed spaces where he could not immediately see how to get out, and that unease followed him into daily life. He was on watch even inside his own home, listening for sounds he could not explain and checking the locks more than once, as if vigilance alone might prevent catastrophe. His wife noticed that he no longer relaxed into an evening meal or a shared television show; part of him seemed always to be somewhere ahead of the moment, calculating how to get clear if something went wrong.

As the months passed, the same harsh conclusions kept feeding that watchfulness. Because he believed he had lost access to normal feeling and that the accident had permanently damaged him, he treated his surroundings as if they were unreliable too. The more he feared that something in him had changed for good, the more determined he became to stay alert for any sign of trouble, and the more he scanned for danger in everyday settings. In the cockpit he had once relied on rapid assessment and control; now he brought that same intensity home, unable to let himself settle. The habit spread outward: at the supermarket he stood near the exit, in the garage he checked what path he would take if he needed to leave quickly, and on the street he watched other people and moving vehicles with a tension that never fully eased. What had begun as a reaction to one emergency became a way of living that left little room for rest.

Tane’s work sharpened the problem. As a combat pilot, he returned to an environment full of alarms, procedural checks, briefing rooms, and tight spaces that could suddenly feel like the beginning of another failure. Even when nothing was wrong, he remained braced, vigilant for cues that might signal danger, and that stance made it harder for him to concentrate or feel present with his squadron. He became quieter with colleagues and more withdrawn with his wife, not because he wanted distance, but because he feared that if he let his guard drop he would miss the first sign that something was about to go wrong. By the time he finally agreed to therapy, he was exhausted by the effort of staying ready all the time and frightened by how much of his life had been reorganized around escape routes and constant surveillance. What he most hoped for was to feel like himself again, and what he feared most was that he had already lost that version of himself for good.
